p: Sandžak covers around 8,500 square kilometres between the south-eastern border of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the borders with Kosovo and Albania. Six of its municipalities are in Serbia (Novi Pazar, Sjenica, Tutin, Prijepolje, Nova Varoš and Priboj) and seven in Montenegro (Pljevlja, Bijelo Polje, Berane, Petnjica, Rožaje, Gusinje and Plav). The name is the Serbo-Croatian form of the Ottoman Turkish sancak, a province; Serbs have historically known the region as Raška, of which it was part in the 12th century.

The Ottoman Empire invaded the Serbian Despotate in 1455. The spread of Islam in Sandžak had several causes: Muslims did not pay the jizya tax or the child levy and were privileged over Christians in administration and the courts; after the Great Turkish War (1683–1699) part of the Orthodox population was driven north and the land was settled by people who were or became Muslim; and the region was a centre of trade. Until 1790 it belonged to the Sanjak of Bosnia, which is why its Muslims identify with the Slavic Muslims of Bosnia.

When Serbian and Montenegrin troops seized the region in October 1912, many Slavic Muslims and Albanians left for Ottoman Turkey. In 1919 an Albanian revolt in the Rožaje, Gusinje and Plav districts against inclusion in the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes was put down; seven hundred Albanians were killed in Rožaje and about 450 civilians in Plav and Gusinje.

In 1941 the region was partitioned between Italian-held Montenegro, the Italian protectorate of Albania and German-occupied Serbia, and Muslim militias, Chetniks and Partisans fought there. On 2 March 1942 the Jews of Novi Pazar were rounded up and killed in camps. In May 1943 Chetnik forces under Pavle Đurišić massacred an estimated 5,400 Albanian men, women and children in Bihor, and an estimated 9,000 Muslims in all were killed by Chetniks and affiliated groups during the war. A Partisan council for Sandžak, founded at Pljevlja on 20 November 1943, accepted on 29 March 1945 the division of the region along the line of 1912.

The municipalities of Sandžak have around 361,656 inhabitants. Bosniaks form 54.8 per cent, Serbs 30 per cent, Montenegrins 5 per cent, people who declare themselves Muslims by ethnicity 3.4 per cent and Albanians 1 per cent. Novi Pazar is the economic and cultural centre. A referendum on autonomy organised by the Muslim National Council of Sandžak between 25 and 27 October 1991 was declared illegal by Serbia. The region remains underdeveloped, and census data show emigration by all its peoples.

notes: Conflict in the article: the lead says the Sanjak of Novi Pazar was 'founded in 1865'; the history says it was separated from the Sanjak of Bosnia in 1790 and joined the Bosnia Vilayet in 1867. I gave only 'until 1790 it belonged to the Sanjak of Bosnia'.
The article's lead dates the Austro-Hungarian garrison 1878-1909; the existing description says 1878-1908. Not repeated here.
The article describes the May 1943 victims in Bihor as Muslims in one sentence and as 'Albanian men, women and children' in the next; I kept the article's wording for the figure.
Left out the 1991 referendum's results, which the article gives only 'according to the SDA' (70.2% turnout, 98.92% in favour).

The article states forced conversion and the devşirme in strong and partly contradictory terms ('periodically and forcefully converted' / 'otherwise caused by ... mainly economic' factors); I gave the three factors it lists.
